title: Unlocking Advanced Time Valuation: Extending ECP with SuccessFactors Time Tracking Start & End Times
author: NeeleshKamath
text:
For years, a data gap between SF Time Tracking and ECP set a hard ceiling on what time valuation could compute. That ceiling has shifted — and the implications go well beyond any single use case 
 The Core Limitation 
 Without start and end time information arriving in ECP: 
 Time evaluation cannot distinguish between two separate 1-hour OT blocks and a single 2-hour block 
 It cannot generate downstream compensatory records that are anchored to the position of the original entry 
 It cannot resolve complex sequences — first occurrence gets one rate, subsequent occurrences get another 

 The result: customers with nuanced labor agreements have consistently run into a wall when configuring time valuation. Requirements get dismissed as "not achievable in standard" not because the logic is unreasonable, but because the data wasn't there to support it. In this blog, we demonstrate with a POC on how to overcome such limitations. Special Thanks to @Jeewan and @suryalakhani0 in this collaboration. It was truly a team effort to create this working prototype and without their efforts, it would not have been possible. 
 In addition, this POC demonstrates the value of an integrated SAP suite and highlights the benefits that SAP products can deliver when working together. It is a testament to the comprehensive suite integration capabilities we provide, setting us apart from our competitors. 

 A Real-World Requirement That Wasn't Possible — Until Now 
 Consider this scenario: a customer allows employees to record overtime multiple times a day after normal working hours. When these OT periods are non-continuous , company policy mandates a make-up rate payment equivalent to a guaranteed 4-hour block. 
 The rule is straightforward: 
 Employee works 1 hour of OT → paid 3 hours at make-up rate (total = 4 hours guaranteed) 
 Employee works 2 hours of OT → paid 2 hours at make-up rate (total = 4 hours guaranteed) 
 This is simple enough for a single OT record. The problem emerges with multiple OT records in the same day. 
 Here's a sample of what the data looks like: 

 Time Pay Type 
 Duration 
 Start Time 
 End Time 
 Notes 

 0M20 - O/time 2.0 rate 
 1.00 hr 
 18:00 
 19:00 
 Recorded in TT 

 0M40 - Make-up 2.0 rate 
 3.00 hrs 
 19:00 
 22:00 
 Generated in time eval 

 0M20 - O/time 2.0 rate 
 0.50 hr 
 19:30 
 20:00 
 Recorded in TT 

 0M40 - Make-up 2.0 rate 
 3.50 hrs 
 20:00 
 23:30 
 Generated in time eval 

 0M20 - O/time 2.0 rate 
 0.75 hr 
 20:15 
 21:00 
 Recorded in TT 

 0M40 - Make-up 2.0 rate 
 3.25 hrs 
 21:00 
 00:15 
 Generated in time eval 

 0M20 - O/time 2.0 rate 
 2.00 hrs 
 23:30 
 01:30 
 Recorded in TT 

 0M40 - Make-up 2.0 rate 
 2.00 hrs 
 01:30 
 03:30 
 Generated in time eval 

 Each OT entry paired with its make-up time represents one complete 4-hour compensation block . The time evaluation engine needs to treat each OT + make-up pair as a discrete, independent unit — not as an aggregate. 
 The core problem: When multiple OT records exist for the same day, time evaluation does not recognize them as 4 unique records. It loses the one-to-one relationship between each overtime entry and its corresponding make-up period. 

 What Changes with Start and End Time Integration 
 The introduction of start and end time data on time type 2010 records flowing from SF Time Tracking into ECP is more than a data enrichment — it is an architectural unlock 
 Previously, ECP time evaluation received duration-only data. A record saying "1 hour of OT" carries no positional information: when did it happen? Does it overlap with another record? Is it genuinely separate? 
 With start and end times now available in ECP: 
 Each OT record has a precise temporal footprint — time evaluation can distinguish between 18:00–19:00 OT and 19:30–20:00 OT as separate events 
 Make-up/Bump up time can be generated individually per OT record , anchored to that record's end time 
 Non-continuous gaps can be detected , enabling policy logic like "this OT block stands alone, therefore it triggers its own 4-hour guarantee" 
 Complex shift patterns become resolvable — night-shift crossings, split-day records, and back-to-back but distinct OT events are no longer ambiguous 
 In short: temporal identity replaces anonymous aggregation , and that changes what time valuation can compute. 

 Why This Matters for E2E POC Design 
 This requirement is an ideal candidate for a Proof of Concept (POC) spanning the full SF TT → ECP chain, precisely because it exercises the boundary that was previously impossible to cross. 
 A well-designed POC here would validate: 
 Data fidelity — do start/end times from TT arrive in ECP accurately, including overnight crossings? 
 Time evaluation logic — can a custom schema handle individual make-up generation per OT record rather than aggregate? 
 Payroll correctness — does the resulting wage type split produce the right gross pay? 
 Scalability — does the logic hold for edge cases like 3, 5, or 6 separate OT blocks in a single day? 

 The Broader Opportunity 
 For years, Time Tracking customers with nuanced overtime policies have had to choose between: 
 Simplifying their policy to match system constraints, or 
 Building complex workarounds in downstream systems 
 The availability of start and end times in ECP removes this trade-off for a meaningful subset of these cases. It moves the boundary of what is achievable in standard configuration — and that is worth documenting, prototyping, and sharing. 
 If your organization has requirements that were previously dismissed as "not possible in standard TT," now is the time to revisit them. 
 This post draws on a real customer scenario that surfaced during discussions on SF TT and ECP integration design. The table above represents a live requirement, not a hypothetical. 

 Configuration in SuccessFactors Time Tracking to enable time valuations with Split Times 

 We created a simple time recording profile to demonstrate this topic and POC 

 These are the time valuations, and the last one is the most interesting one. It fetches OT for a given day 

 The Time Type Group above, which is Overtime 150%, is the final output and has split by clock times enabled. This ensures that each occurrence of overtime, which is non-continuous, is captured separately in the time valuation results 

 Examples of time Recording 
 Let’s look at some examples of time recording for a user, Martin Smith. The employee works an 8 AM to 5 PM shift 
 In the week of Jan 9, 2026, the employee has two instances of overtime recorded separately, as seen below 

 And below are the time valuation results split by clock times. As you see there are two instances now for the OT 150% 

 And also, with start and end times 

 Similarly we have Overtime also recorded in next week. In this case again we have 2 separate occurrences of overtime on Jan 13, but one overtime event is already greater than 4 hours (i.e 5 hours). This occurrence will not be bumped up in ECP 

 Now let’s look at the Payroll Configurations and how the results from above-mentioned valuations can be extended in ECP using the above information like start and end times that is replicated to 2010 
 Payroll Configurations and Test Results 
 Create a wage type and ensure that the valuation basis is correctly defined for this wage type in table V_512W_B. In our example, we have configured to apply 150% i.e. pay at 1.5 times the daily rate. 

 Maintain the code value mapping - the external code of the Time Pay Type to Wage Type in table T77SFEC_CVMAPC ( or follow the IMG path whatever works for you 😉 ) 

 Create a Constant in Payroll Constant in table (V_T511K) - This allows you to manage the threshold value as an effective dated entry. 

 Create a PCR: It is a simple PCR that allows you to read the wage type and evaluate if the overtime hours for each occurrence of the wage type per day is less than the threshold value. If so, bump it up to the threshold value. 
 Note: You can also write custom ABAP functions on payroll side if PCR does not meet your needs. Its quite flexible 

 Add the PCR immediately after the function 2010 is read in GT00. This will ensure the standard PCR G015 adds the correct rate to the wage type as per the valuation basis configured for the wage type. 

 All done. 
 Let’s look at the example 

 You can see that in IT2010 for the employee all four records are replicated successfully but the start time and end time for the record is not visible in the overview screen. 

 If you evaluate the records using database table PA2010, you can see the start and end times are replicated as well. 

 During the payroll run, function P2010 is reading these entries for each occurrence of the overtime on the same day is uniquely identified. The output of the P2010 you can see the the variable assignment type and variable assignment number assigned to these records for the wage type 1235. 

 Custom PCR that was configured previously and called immediately after function P2010 applies the threshold and updates the hours during the payroll run, as you see below. 

 The standard PCR G015 valuate the wage type and assigns the correct rate to the wage types. In our example 150% of /001 (per the wage type valuation basis configuration) 

 And finally, the payslip, displays the valuation hours. 

 Please note; ECP should have May 2026 HR Synchronization package applied in particular SAP note 3585805 should be applied to replicate the start and end time in IT2010. 
 In summary: This new integration mechanism now unlocks a lot of opportunities to build E2E Time valuation aspects with payroll. And a lot of upsell opportunities for sales too 😉 
 We hope this helps you in complex implementation projects 
 Best Regards 
 Neelesh Kamath, Jeewan Patni and Surya Lakhani

title: Make It Work: Configuring Crowd Integration Across SAP S/4HANA and SAP FSA
author: sureshmusham
text:
This post is for the consultants and administrators who are actually setting up the Crowd Workforce Integration between SAP S/4HANA and SAP FSA. Part 1 of this series covered the business problem and how the integration works end to end. Here we get into the specifics: what to configure, in which system, in what order, and what to check when you're done. 
 Blog Series: 
 Part 1: Crowd Integration Between S/4HANA and FSA -- Business Context, Solution Architecture, How it Works 
 Part 2: Make It Work: Configuring Crowd Integration Across S/4HANA and FSA 
 We cover two deployment scenarios. Scenario A is the standard setup where technicians are replicated from S/4HANA service performers. Scenario B is the variant — used when the crowd partner wants to manage their own technicians directly in FSA without a corresponding employee record in S/4HANA. 
 Prerequisites at a Glance 

 System 
 Object / Setting 
 Action 
 Why It Matters 

 SAP S/4HANA 
 Business Function /SHCM/EE_BP_1 
 Activate in Switch Framework (transaction SFW5) 
 Enables the Service Performer partner function BBP005 and BUR025 relationship type for Business Partners while converting the Employee to Business Partner 

 SAP S/4HANA 
 SAP Note 0002882172 
 Review and apply as required 
 Documents known issues and corrections related to the /SHCM/EE_BP_1 Business Function activation 

 SAP S/4HANA 
 Item Category for External Service Item 
 SRVW (or SREW for returns) configured in service order customising 
 Identifies service order items as external — triggers PR creation and FSA activity with subtype 'External Service 

 SAP S/4HANA 
 Lean Service Procurement 
 Standard lean service integration between SM and MM configured 
 Required for automatic PR creation on service order release 

 SAP BTP / CPI 
 SAP S/4HANA–FSA integration package 
 Already deployed and active 
 Crowd integration extends the existing iFlows — it does not replace them 

 SAP FSA 
 Crowd Workforce module 
 Licensed and enabled in the FSA tenant 
 Required for Crowd Partner and Technician objects to exist in FSA 

 SAP FSA 
 Crowd Partner Portal 
 Enabled in FSA tenant configuration 
 External crowd partners need portal access for assignment acceptance and EMME approval 
 Scenario A: Standard Setup — Technicians Replicated from S/4HANA 
 This is the default scenario. Everything flows from S/4HANA: the supplier, their workers, and all field activity assignments are traceable back to S/4HANA records. Use this when the customer wants S/4HANA as the single system of record for both the supplier relationship and the individual technicians. 
 Step 1 — Activate Business Function /SHCM/EE_BP_1 
 Go to transaction SFW5 in S/4HANA. Locate Business Function /SHCM/EE_BP_1 and activate it. This is a permanent, irreversible activation — confirm with the customer before proceeding. Once activated, it makes the following available: 
 Partner function BBP005 (Service Performer) for use in Business Partner relationships 
 Relationship type BUR025 (Employee — has Service Performer) between a person BP and a company BP 
 The person type 'Contingent Worker' on Employee BPs, which generates the Service Performer BP role on BP conversion 
 Important: Review SAP Note 0002882172 before activating. It covers known corrections for this Business Function that may apply to your release level. 
 If Customer uses Employee Group other than “9” for contingent worker than a BADi implementation is required. Reference blog: External Workforce in Employee Business Partner Data Model 
 Use the synchronization reports ( /SHCM/RH_SYNC_BUPA_EMPL_SINGLE or /SHCM/RH_SYNC_BUPA_FROM_EMPL ), to sync created employees as Business Partner with role BUP003 and BBP005. 

 Step 2 — Configure Partner Function BBP005 for Relationship Type BUR025 
 Create your supplier as a Business Partner (transaction FLVN01) with the relevant purchasing organisation and currency. Then link the service performers to this supplier using relationship type BUR025 — Has Service Performer. 

 That's the trigger. Once those relationships are saved, the new CPI iFlow — "Replicate Crowd Partner and Technician from SAP S/4HANA to SAP Field Service and Asset Management" — picks them up automatically and creates the Crowd Partner and Crowd Technicians in FSA. Adding or removing service performers later is handled the same way — the changes flow through to FSA Crowd Workforce without any manual intervention. 
 One thing that must be in place before replication runs: make sure a valid address dependent email is maintained on both the Supplier BP and each Employee BP. FSA requires an email address to create Crowd Partner and Technician records — it's how the platform sends onboarding notifications to the crowd partner. Missing emails will stop the replication. 
 If you don't want to maintain individual technicians in S/4HANA, there's a configuration option for that. Set the iFlow external parameter “CrowdPartner W/O Service Performer” to true. In this mode, the supplier replicates to FSA as a Crowd Partner with a placeholder technician carrying the supplier's details. The crowd partner admin then manages their own technicians directly in FSA. This is the right choice when the customer wants to keep their external workforce data out of S/4HANA entirely. 
 Role Mapping: Crowd Admin vs Crowd Technician: employees created with both Employee and Contingent Worker person types get both the Crowd Admins roles in FSA. 
 Step 3 — Configure Item Category for External Service Items 
 In Customizing path “ SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Service -> Transactions -> Basic Settings -> Define Item Category Determination ” , ensure the item category SRVW and SREW are configured and assigned to the relevant order type (SRVO) and item category group (SRVP or DIEN). 
 With this you can add External Service item categories to the Service Order. 
 In Customer path “ SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Service -> Transactions Settings for Service Transactions -> Integration -> Logistics Integration -> Enterprise Organizational Management -> Define Logistics Scenario for Procurement of Materials and Services”, for the Purchase Requisition to auto create on the External Service Item, add PREQ as logistic. 
 If you are using legacy org, then patch will “ SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Service -> Transactions Settings for Service Transactions -> Integration -> Logistics Integration -> Organizational Management(Legacy) -> Define Logistics Scenario for Procurement of Materials and Services” 

 Step 4 — Add Vendor and Service Performer Parties in Service 
 To update the Vendor and External technician to the External service item, maintain Vendor (0000019) and Service Performer (0000028) functions against Ext. Service Item (00000032) & Ext. Confirmation Service Item (00000033) categories in the Partner Function determination in Service. 
 Customizing path: “ SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Service -> Basic Functions -> Partner Processing -> Define Partner Determination Procedure in Service ” 

 Step 5: Authorization to access Purchase apps: 
 Make sure you have below roles to view purchase orders, requisition and service entry sheet 
 SAP_BR_EMPLOYEE_PROCUREMENT, SAP_BR_PURCHASER. SAP_BR_INTERNAL_SALES_REP 
 Step 6: Maintain Purchasing Info Record: 
 Maintain mapping of Purchase Org and Plant with the Service Material and Supplier in Purchasing Info Record (tcode ME11). This is required to create purchase order using purchase requisition. 

 Step 7 — Configure the CPI iFlows 
 In SAP BTP Integration Suite, open the standard package “SAP S/4HANA Integration with SAP Field Service and Assent Management”. The four iFlows relevant to crowd integration are: 
 Replicate Service Order from SAP S4HANA to SAP Field Service and Asset Management SOAP — sends service order and external service item to FSA on release. Configure “External Service Item Categories” as SRVW,SREW. 
 Notify External Service Order Item with Crowd Changes from SAP Field Service and Asset Management to SAP S4HANA – sends all crowd updates to external item. 
 Crowd Service Entry Sheet Creation from SAP Field Service and Asset Management to SAP S4HANA – creates Service Entry Sheet on activity confirmations on external activity. 
 Route Payload from SAP Field Service and Asset Management to SAP S/4HANA — handles all inbound FSA crowd events 
 Step 8 —FSA Connector Events for Crowd Business Events 
 The crowd business events mentioned below will be routed through the FSM Connector outbound event to initiate CPI endpoint. There is not configuration required, this will be taken care by standard in FSA. 

 Event 
 When It Fires 
 What It Triggers in S/4HANA 

 crowd.activity.assigned and accepted 
 Crowd partner accepts assignment in Partner Portal 
 Updates Vendor and Service Performer on S/4HANA service order item 

 crowd.activity.released 
 Crowd partner releases activity for field execution 
 Triggers automatic PO creation in S/4HANA via FSMIMPORT 

 crowd.activity.cancelled 
 Assignment cancelled by crowd partner 
 Updates service order status in S/4HANA 

 crowd.activity.unassigned 
 Activity unassigned from crowd resource 
 Clears assignment data from S/4HANA service order item 

 EMME time effort approved 
 activity.confirmed on external activity 
 Crowd admin approves time effort booking 
 Creates SES (for time effort) + auto-approves + triggers Service Confirmation in S/4HANA 
 Create Service Confirmations for other non-time EMME’s like Expenses, Mileages, & Material 
 Step 9 — Enable the Crowd Workforce Module in FSA 
 In FSA, go to Admin → Company Settings and verify that the Crowd module is enabled. 
 For details, refer to  Configure Single Tenant Crowd . 
 Scenario B - Technicians Managed Only in FSA 
 Some customers want to onboard their external suppliers as crowd partners in FSA but don't want to maintain individual technician records in S/4HANA. The supplier manages their own workforce directly in FSA. 
 To achieve this, follow below handling in the configurations: 
 In the CPI iFlow parameters, configure “CrowdPartner W/O Service Performer” parameter as true in below iflows 
 Replicate Business Partner 
 Replicate Crowd Partner and Technician from SAP S4HANA to SAP Field Service and Asset Management 
 Crowd Service Entry Sheet Creation from SAP Field Service and Asset Management to SAP S4HANA 
 Notify External Service Order Item with Crowd Changes from SAP Field Service and Asset Management to SAP S4HANA 
 The effects of that single flag change: 
 The Supplier BP still replicates to FSA as a Crowd Partner — the company-level entity is created 
 No Crowd Technicians or Admins are created from S/4HANA service performer relationships 
 The crowd partner admin creates and manages their own technicians directly in FSA 
 When the crowd partner accepts and releases assignments, S/4HANA receives the status update (In Execution) but not the Executing Service Employee nor Service Performer. 
 Note that email is maintained on the Supplier in this scenario as well. 
 Scenario Comparison 

 Capability 
 Scenario A — Standard 
 Scenario B — Without Technician S4HANA 

 Technician data in S/4HANA 
 Required (employee BPs with BUR025 relationship) 
 Not required 

 Crowd Technician creation 
 Automatic from S/4HANA service performer replication 
 Manual, directly in FSA by crowd partner admin 

 Technician identity in S/4HANA 
 Visible on service order Parties Involved 
 Not populated (status update only) 

 Executing Employee on Confirmation 
 Actual technician from FSA assignment 
 Fallback to service order creator 

 Best for 
 Customers who manage supplier workforce in S/4HANA and want full traceability 
 Customers who let suppliers self-manage their teams in FSA 
 EMME Processing: Two Paths, One Clear Rule 
 When a technician books work through the FSA EMME journal, the integration handles different entry types differently. This is worth understanding explicit

title: From Cold Lead to Qualified Opportunity in Minutes:SAP Sales Cloud V2's Deal Qualification Assistant
author: Yogananda
text:
Sales pipelines live and die by the quality of leads entering them. Yet for most sales teams, lead qualification remains one of the most time-intensive and inconsistently executed steps in the entire sales cycle. Reps research prospects manually, apply their own judgment about fit, and make conversion decisions without a shared standard. The result: pipelines bloated with low-quality leads, reps spending hours on research instead of selling, and opportunities slipping through the cracks. 
 SAP Sales Cloud V2's Deal Qualification Assistant is built to change that — fundamentally. 
 What Is the Deal Qualification Assistant? 
 The Deal Qualification Assistant is a set of coordinated AI agents embedded directly in SAP Sales Cloud V2. It acts as an orchestrating assistant capable of triggering multiple agents simultaneously — an enrichment agent, a qualification agent, and a conversion agent — each delivering distinct value at specific stages of the lead lifecycle. 
 The goal is straightforward: help sales teams focus on the leads most likely to become valuable opportunities, while reducing the manual effort required to get there. 

 How to enable Agent in your SAP Sales Cloud v2 tenant? 

 The Problem It Solves: Manual Work at Scale 
 Consider a typical scenario. A new lead arrives in the CRM — a company name, a contact, maybe a job title. Without richer context, it's nearly impossible for a rep to engage meaningfully, let alone make a sound qualification decision. Traditionally, a rep would spend five to ten minutes per lead browsing the web, cross-referencing LinkedIn, and pulling together enough information to make a first call worthwhile. 
 Multiply that across hundreds of leads per week, and the inefficiency becomes staggering. Worse, each rep brings their own research habits and qualification instincts, creating inconsistency across the team. 
 How It Works: A Stage-by-Stage Walkthrough 
 Stage 1 — Instant Lead Enrichment 
 With a single click, the Enrichment Agent gets to work. It automatically loads the lead record with: 
 Firmographic data — company size, industry, revenue, geography 
 Relevant sales signals — buying intent indicators, recent business events 
 Contextual background — company information and market positioning that doesn't fit neatly into standard CRM fields 
 The lead data model updates in real time, and the timeline section provides a transparent audit trail of exactly what the AI has added or changed. This includes unstructured data — company background narratives, buying signals, and other qualitative intelligence — surfaced alongside structured field updates. 
 The result: an Enrichment Score of 100% in seconds, achieved without a rep leaving the CRM. 
 Because enrichment is saved at the lead level, every rep on the team — and every subsequent agent in the workflow — works from the same data foundation. There's no duplicated research, no knowledge locked in one person's browser history. 
 Stage 2 — ICP Fit Scoring and Lead Acceptance 
 Once the lead is enriched, the Qualification Agent evaluates it against your organisation's Ideal Customer Profile (ICP) . This produces a Fitment Score — a quantified measure of how well the prospect matches the criteria your team has defined as indicative of pipeline-worthy leads. 
 In practice, a lead scoring 70 or above advances automatically to an Accepted status. Leads that don't meet the threshold are filtered out early, before they consume a rep's time. 
 This step transforms qualification from an individual judgment call into a consistent, criteria-driven process applied uniformly across every lead in the system. 
 Stage 3 — Engagement Signals and Dynamic Re-assessment 
 Lead qualification isn't a one-time event. As the sales rep begins interacting with the prospect — gathering information on needs, budget, and strategic fit — those interactions are captured in the lead timeline. Emails, meeting notes, discovery call outcomes: all of it feeds back into the assistant. 
 When the Deal Qualification Assistant is invoked again after these interactions have accumulated, it reassesses the lead in light of new engagement data. A lead showing strong buying signals and meaningful engagement can advance to a Hot status, with the assistant surfacing a proposal to convert the lead — automatically creating an Account and Contact in the background, with clear reasoning provided for why the conversion is recommended. 
 No navigating through separate menus. No manual data re-entry. The firmographic enrichment performed by the enrichment agent cascades directly into the newly created account, becoming the baseline reference going forward. 
 Stage 4 — Discovery Surveys and Calculated Qualification Scores 
 Many organisations structure their discovery process around a formal survey — capturing qualification criteria in a consistent format across every deal. SAP Sales Cloud V2 integrates this seamlessly. 
 Survey responses feed into a calculated qualification score , and the Deal Qualification Assistant takes that score into account as part of its overall assessment. This means structured discovery data — the kind typically buried in spreadsheets or shared drives — becomes a live input to the AI's qualification logic. 
 Stage 5 — Opportunity Creation with a Ready Briefing 
 When the conditions are right, the assistant proposes converting the lead into a formal Opportunity . Accepting that proposal moves the lead to a Converted status — the logical endpoint of the lead record — and the successor opportunity is created automatically. 
 Critically, all lead data carries over to the opportunity, and a summary is auto-generated for the account executive taking over. Rather than digging through every prior interaction, the AE receives a ready briefing: context, signals, qualification rationale, and next steps — all in one place. 
 The Business Impact 
 The value of the Deal Qualification Assistant compounds quickly when you think at scale: 
 Without Deal Qualification Assistant With Deal Qualification Assistant 
 5–10 min per lead for manual research Instant enrichment with a single click 
 Qualification based on individual judgment Consistent ICP-driven fitment scoring 
 Static qualification — assessed once Dynamic reassessment as engagement evolves 
 Manual account/contact creation at conversion Automated creation with cascaded data 
 AE onboarding requires reading through all prior interactions Auto-generated opportunity summary for immediate context 
 Agentic AI in Practice 
 What makes the Deal Qualification Assistant particularly significant is its agentic architecture . Rather than a single AI model generating a recommendation, it coordinates multiple specialised agents — each with a defined scope and trigger — that can operate simultaneously or in sequence depending on the state of the lead. 
 This is a meaningful shift from traditional AI-assisted CRM features. The system doesn't just surface insights; it takes contextually appropriate actions , updates records, creates downstream objects, and adapts its recommendations as new information becomes available. The rep remains in control — reviewing and accepting proposals — but the cognitive and administrative load shifts dramatically. 
 Closing Thoughts 
 The Deal Qualification Assistant represents a practical, high-impact application of agentic AI in enterprise sales. It addresses a problem every sales organisation faces — too many leads, not enough context, inconsistent qualification — with a solution that is embedded directly in the workflow rather than bolted on as a separate tool. 
 For Sales Development Managers , the promise is a healthier pipeline fed by a process that is faster, more consistent, and more transparent than anything a manual approach can deliver. For account executives, it means inheriting opportunities with the context they need to hit the ground running. 
 The technology is here. The question is how quickly your team puts it to work.

title: Discrepancy in DMEE Format Name Displayed in F110 DME Administration
author: KiranBabuR
text:
Hi Team, 
 We have created a new DMEE format Z_CITI_CN_CGI_XML_CT_1 by copying the existing DMEE format Z_CITI_CN_CGI_XML_CT .

title: planning calendar at supplier level
author: augustobeda
text:
Subject: Supplier planning calendar in BP purchasing data: impact on MRP and PP/DS in S/4HANA (multi-source scenario) 
 Hello, 
 We are analyzing how supplier-specific calendars can be handled in planning in S/4HANA (embedded PP/DS), and we would like to clarify the following points. 
 Context 
 System: S/4HANA release [version], embedded PP/DS 
 Scenario: multi-source procurement (several vendors per material, source list / quota arrangements) 
 Requirement: scheduling of external procurement proposals should take into account the vendor’s non-working days (e.g. summer shutdown), instead of using calendar days only 
 What we understood so far 
 MRP schedules external procurement using the planned delivery time (calendar days) against the Gregorian calendar, not a vendor factory calendar. 
 The only workaround we identified is periodic lot-sizing with an MRP planning calendar, but this is assigned at material master level and therefore only works in a single-source scenario. 
 Questions 
 The planning calendar can be maintained in the vendor’s purchasing data (Business Partner / supplier purchasing organization data). Is this calendar read by MRP or PP/DS in any scenario? If so, under which conditions (e.g. lot-sizing procedure, scheduling agreements, delivery schedules)? 
 If it has no impact on MRP/PP/DS scheduling, which functions does it support (e.g. order cycles in purchasing, release creation for scheduling agreements)? 
 Is there any standard way in S/4HANA (embedded PP/DS) to consider a vendor-specific working calendar when scheduling procurement proposals in a multi-source scenario? 
 If not, what is the recommended workaround (e.g. vendor-specific planned delivery time adjusted ahead of shutdown periods, custom enhancement, BAdI)? Please indicate any relevant SAP Notes or documentation. 
 Thank you in advance for your support. 
 Best regards, 
 Augusto Beda

title: 10 Questions Board Members Should Be Asking About Security and Compliance
author: Marielle Ehrmann
text:
Major security incidents can quickly affect enterprise value, operational continuity, regulatory standing, and reputation. 
 Securely access cloud services, meet compliance goals, and build customer confidence 

 Learn how 

 As organizations become more dependent on connected infrastructure, cloud services, AI, and third parties, weaknesses in one part of the ecosystem can cascade across the business. 

 A Board is not expected to make technical decisions. Its role is to exercise informed oversight: set expectations, test whether accountability is clear, require evidence of resilience, and ensure that management integrates security and compliance into strategy, investment, operations, and crisis preparedness. 

 The following questions are designed for a Board of Directors and its relevant committees. They broaden the original cybersecurity focus to include compliance, privacy, data governance, third-party assurance, regulatory change, and demonstrable control effectiveness. 

 1. Are security and compliance roles, decision rights, and escalation paths clearly defined? 

 Treating security or compliance as an isolated specialist function weakens governance. Accountability should extend across executive leadership, business operations, technology, legal, risk, privacy, internal audit, and the security organization. The Board should understand who owns material risks, what is the risk appetite who can accept them, and how significant incidents, control failures, vulnerabilities, or regulatory concerns reach the appropriate committee or full Board. 

 Evidence to request : 

 Does the security and compliance leadership team have direct access to executive management and the Board? 

 Are material risks escalated before they materialize into active incidents? 

 Do responsibilities cover prevention, detection, response, recovery, regulatory obligations, and assurance? 

 2. Are security and compliance built into strategy, investment, and transformation decisions? 

 Security and compliance should shape strategic choices from the beginning, not be added after commitments have been made. Major investments, cloud programs, acquisitions, new products, AI initiatives, and supplier selections should be assessed alongside security and compliance considerations. Early involvement helps identify structural risk while decisions are still practical to change. 

 Evidence to request : 

 Which strategic decisions require a documented security and compliance review? 

 What risks or control requirements influenced the final decision? 

 Are funding and accountability aligned with the risk created by the initiative? 

 3. Do we have a transparent, decision-ready view of security and compliance risk? 

 Boards need more than technical activity reports. Management should translate important threats, vulnerabilities, control gaps, legal obligations, and business dependencies into clear enterprise risk scenarios. Reporting should show potential operational, financial, legal, and reputational consequences, as well as the residual risk that remains after controls are applied. 

 Evidence to request: 

 Which scenarios could materially affect our strategic objectives? 

 How are likelihood, business impact, and control effectiveness assessed? 

 What residual risks have been accepted, by whom, and for how long? 

 4. Is our compliance strategy prepared for regulatory change? 

 Compliance should be managed as a continuing capability rather than a periodic response to individual requirements. The Board should assess whether regulatory developments are monitored, interpreted consistently, assigned to accountable owners, and translated into controls, technology roadmaps, evidence, and reporting. This includes requirements affecting security, privacy, data sovereignty, operational resilience, AI, and third-party services. 

 Evidence to request: 

 Which emerging requirements could materially affect the business? 

 How quickly can new obligations be translated into operational controls? 

 Can management demonstrate compliance consistently across regions, business units, and technology environments? 

 5. Are legacy systems and technical debt creating unacceptable security or compliance exposure? 

 Systems that are no longer fully supported can accumulate security weaknesses, limit monitoring, complicate recovery, and make compliance evidence harder to produce. The Board should view aging critical systems as an enterprise risk and investment issue, not just an IT lifecycle matter. Where modernization is delayed, management should document compensating controls, ownership, and a time-bound plan. 

 Evidence to request: 

 Which critical systems are out of support or approaching end of support? 

 What business processes and regulatory obligations depend on them? 

 What is the modernization plan and how is interim risk independently validated? 

 6. Are AI security, compliance, and governance embedded in the operating model? 

 AI introduces security, legal, privacy, data, ethical, and operational questions that require coordinated governance. Whether AI is developed internally or obtained from a third party, management should know what data it can access, how outputs are used, which decisions remain subject to human review, and how systems are tested and monitored as they change. 

 Evidence to request: 

 Who is accountable for approving and monitoring AI use cases? 

 What controls protect sensitive data and prevent unauthorized use? 

 How are legal, ethical, security, compliance, and human-rights considerations evaluated and evidenced? 

 7. Are identity and access management strong enough for our risk profile? 

 Compromised credentials and excessive access can allow attackers or insiders to reach critical systems and data. Identity and access management should be treated as a business control, not simply an administrative technology process. Strong governance connects employee, contractor, third-party, and system identities to reliable business records and removes access when it is no longer required. 

 Evidence to request: 

 Are strong authentication and least-privilege access applied to critical systems? 

 How quickly is access changed when roles, employment, or supplier relationships change? 

 Are privileged and non-human identities monitored, reviewed, and time-limited where appropriate? 

 8. Does our culture measurably reduce human and conduct risk? 

 Policies and technical controls depend on people making sound decisions. A mature program goes beyond annual training by addressing role-specific exposure, leadership behavior, phishing and social engineering, secure ways of working, speak-up channels, and consequences for repeated noncompliance. The Board should seek measurable evidence that behavior and risk are improving. 

 Evidence to request: 

 Which roles face the highest security and compliance exposure? 

 What do simulations, incidents, training results, and behavioral indicators show over time? 

 How visibly do leaders reinforce expected behavior and accountability? 

 9. Are third-party and supply-chain risks continuously assessed and governed? 

 Security and compliance obligations do not stop at the enterprise boundary. Critical suppliers, cloud providers, software dependencies, advisers, and other partners can create operational, regulatory, data, concentration, and geopolitical exposure. Third-party risk should be integrated into enterprise risk management and monitored throughout the relationship, not treated as a one-time procurement exercise. 

 Evidence to request: 

 Which third parties are critical to operations, data, or regulatory obligations? 

 What independent evidence supports their security, compliance, and resilience claims? 

 How are concentration, subcontractor, geographic, and exit risks managed? 

 10. Are we prepared to detect, contain, disclose, and recover from a major incident? 

 Prevention alone is not enough. The Board should understand whether the organization can identify significant events early, contain their impact, make timely legal and regulatory decisions, communicate credibly, restore priority services, and learn from the event. Readiness should cover ransomware, account takeover, data compromise, fraud, third-party disruption, and other plausible business scenarios. 

 Evidence to request: 

 When were crisis, incident response, business continuity, and recovery plans last exercised together? 

 Are decision rights clear for regulatory disclosure, law enforcement, ransom demands, customer communication, and service restoration? 

 What gaps were found in recent exercises or incidents, and are remediation actions closed? 

 From reactive oversight to demonstrable resilience 

 These 10 questions help a Board move the discussion from technical activity to governance, accountability, evidence, and business outcomes. Effective oversight requires an ongoing dialogue with management, constructive challenge of assumptions, and decisions that reflect the organization’s risk profile, regulatory obligations, and digital maturity. 

 Modernization can be an important governance lever when it improves standardization, transparency, control automation, resilience, and the ability to produce reliable compliance evidence. Responsibility, however, remains shared across leaders, business owners, technology teams, security, compliance, legal, risk, audit, employees, and critical partners. 

 Board takeaway 

 Security and compliance are not separate from business strategy. They are essential to continuity, lawful operation, stakeholder trust, and long-term value protection. 

 Marielle Ehrmann is chief security officer and a member of the Supervisory Board of SAP SE.

title: From Two Weeks to Seconds: How Ericsson Is Reimagining B2B Commerce with AI
author: Jin Oh
text:
In many B2B organizations, creating a customer quote still involves a familiar sequence of emails, approvals, contract reviews, and manual handoffs. The process can take days or even weeks, creating delays for customers and additional work for employees. 
 Generate traffic from AI search and use AI to execute 

 Learn how 

 Ericsson knows this challenge well. 

 As a global leader in telecommunications technology operating in more than 190 countries, Ericsson manages highly complex commercial relationships involving products, services, customer-specific contracts, pricing agreements, and global fulfillment operations. Behind every quote is a web of business rules, approvals, and dependencies that must be coordinated accurately and efficiently. 

 For years, that complexity created friction in the quoting process. In some cases, generating a quote could take more than two weeks. Today, many of those same requests can be completed in minutes or even seconds. 

 The hidden complexity behind every quote 

 At Ericsson, many customer transactions are tied to multi-year framework agreements that include negotiated pricing, contract-specific products, and customer entitlements. Sometimes customers return months or even years after an agreement is signed and need to understand what products, configurations, and pricing are available to them before placing an order. 

 Historically, that process often required customers to contact their account representative, who would manually gather information, validate contract terms, and prepare a quote. Depending on the complexity of the request, responses could take days or even weeks. 

 Ericsson’s objective was straightforward: make it easier for customers to do business with the company. 

 “We want to be easier to work with as a partner to our customers,” said Aaron Thomas, global product owner at Ericsson. 

 Using SAP Commerce Cloud , Ericsson introduced digital commerce capabilities that allow customers to access contract-specific products, generate quotes, and place orders through self-service channels. Customers can now access dedicated storefronts built around their agreements, browse available products, generate quotes, and complete transactions without relying on manual intervention from account teams. 

 What once took days or weeks can now be completed in minutes or even seconds, helping improve accuracy and reduce rework across commercial operations. 

 Beyond automation: Exploring the role of AI agents 

 Once the quoting process became digitized and streamlined, Ericsson began exploring how AI could take commercial execution to the next level. 

 “We’ve moved from manual processes to digitized and automated processes,” Thomas explained. “Now we’re asking: can an agent perform those tasks?” 

 Rather than using AI solely as a productivity tool, the company started evaluating how AI agents could actively participate in commercial processes. 

 One area Ericsson is exploring is quote creation. The company is evaluating how AI agents could analyze customer requests, identify relevant contract information, assemble recommendations, and prepare proposed quotes for human review. 

 Employees remain responsible for oversight and decision-making, while AI helps reduce administrative work and allows sales and account teams to spend more time advising customers, solving business challenges, and strengthening relationships. 

 The company is also exploring other AI-driven capabilities, including agents that can improve product descriptions and search experiences across its internal product portfolio, helping employees find information more quickly across a large and complex catalog. 

 Defining the next chapter of B2B commerce 

 For Ericsson, AI is becoming more than a productivity tool. It is creating new possibilities for how commercial work gets done. 

 Reducing quote creation from weeks to seconds delivered immediate value for customers and employees alike. But the company’s exploration of AI agents points to a broader shift, one where intelligent systems help businesses execute complex processes faster, more consistently, and at greater scale. 

 For Ericsson, the journey from weeks-long quoting cycles to AI-assisted execution is about more than efficiency. It is about creating a simpler experience for customers and helping employees focus on the work that matters most. As the company continues exploring how agents can support commercial operations, it is helping redefine how complex B2B processes can be executed in the age of AI. 

 To learn more about Ericsson’s approach to AI and the future of agentic commerce, watch the webinar: Agentic B2B Commerce: Finding the fast track to profitable growth . You can also explore SAP’s vision for unified commerce at sap.com/unified-commerce and learn how organizations are connecting commerce, customer experiences, and operational execution to drive better business outcomes.
